all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: virtual reality
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.

The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

The flight simulator concept introduced for the first time in 1928 by Edwin A. Link evolved into sophisticated flight simulators with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience, and this early development is considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality (VR).

The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.
The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

Cyber sickness can be independent of age when users view general virtual reality (VR) content, while age may be a factor for controllable content, making the age relationship clearer for controllable content.

A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

Virtual reality (VR) recreates realistic movement and visual environments, making the user feel as if in a real-world environment; therefore, users with motion sickness (MS) susceptibility tend also to have cyber sickness susceptibility.

Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.
Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.
An understanding of human perception is needed to design a better virtual reality (VR) system or to identify and resolve flaws in a given system.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: virtual tour
concepts.definition: Experiencing heritage in the virtual reality (VR) system for Majuli River Island is intended as an immersive virtual tour or exploration of Majuli River Island that uses the archive of heritage information.

defining_facts.text: Experiencing heritage in the virtual reality (VR) system for Majuli River Island is intended as an immersive virtual tour or exploration of Majuli River Island that uses the archive of heritage information.

The digital heritage preservation system for Majuli island has two components: preservation, which produces the content of the virtual tour, and experiencing the heritage through immersive virtual tours, which allow users to explore the island virtually.

Majuli island's distinct tribal cultures are present in tribal villages that dot the landscape, its three major tribes are Mishing, Deori, and Sonowal Kacharis, each of which is supposed to have a distinct tangible and intangible cultural identity, and the villages' unique traditions and customs should be reproduced in a virtual tour.

concepts.name: cybersickness
concepts.definition: Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

defining_facts.text: Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

A large number of symptoms may indicate the onset of cybersickness (CS) or cybersickness itself, and common ones include nausea, headache, excessive sweating, dryness of mouth, fullness of stomach, vomiting or a tendency to vomit, dizziness, disorientation, fatigue, and strange hand-eye coordination in which coordination does not happen in the expected way, so if one or more of these symptoms occur during a virtual reality (VR) experience, cybersickness can be assumed to be happening or going to happen.
Cybersickness (CS) can be caused by many factors, not by a single factor.

Reducing the impact of cybersickness (CS) is very important for usability and acceptability of virtual reality (VR) systems because it greatly enhances overall user experience and makes virtual reality applications more appealing to a wider range of people.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.

A sensory mismatch in a virtual reality (VR) system may be insignificant if the user's brain can adapt, but for other users it can cause cybersickness, with symptoms such as fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea.

Cybersickness, also known as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR), and it is not a single-factor effect because a variety of factors can affect it.

The factors that can induce cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, which include the age of the user, the gender of the user, the user's susceptibility to motion sickness, the physical condition of the user, and the emotional condition of the user, and external factors, which include hardware factors such as display resolution, latency, latency jitter, type of display, and type of input, and virtual reality (VR) content factors such as visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

Finding feasible solutions to reduce the impact of cybersickness while a user is experiencing virtual reality (VR) is important because it is supposed to greatly enhance overall user experience and make VR more appealing to a wider range of people.

Cybersickness mitigation strategies often come at the cost of presence because reducing cybersickness may make the user feel more in an artificial environment than in a real environment and less likely to obtain a proper immersive experience.

concepts.name: node
concepts.definition: A scene graph is a node-based graph, essentially a tree of nodes and links, that represents a computer graphics scene, allowing selective work with nodes to manipulate the scene, create realistic effects, and support interaction, thereby providing a way to manage the functionality of a complex graphics application.

defining_facts.text: A scene graph is a node-based graph, essentially a tree of nodes and links, that represents a computer graphics scene, allowing selective work with nodes to manipulate the scene, create realistic effects, and support interaction, thereby providing a way to manage the functionality of a complex graphics application.

In a scene-graph representation of the marker-cow augmented reality (AR) example, the whole activity is represented as a node graph containing nodes for video input, tracking, a root node, a virtual camera whose parameters can be manipulated, projection, other related concepts, the three-dimensional (3D) object, and transformations represented as a single node or individual nodes; video input comes from the input device, tracking uses device sensors such as a camera, and graphics-rendering nodes include transformation, three-dimensional (3D) object representation, and orthographic projection, making the scene easier to visualize and manipulate to create the desired effect.
In the virtual reality path optimization model, each node has two associated quantities: importance and waiting time.

In the virtual reality path optimization formulation, the waiting time at a node, which is a point of interest, is the maximum time a user requires to inspect or interact with the object at that node, and it is represented by a waiting-time function W that maps each node v in V to a positive real number.
For a path P with vertices v1 to vn, the total waiting time W(P) is the sum of the individual waiting times W(v_i) for i = 1 to n.

concepts.name: contextual inquiry
concepts.definition: Contextual inquiry is one of many methods for gathering end-user requirements, which in the context of usability requirement gathering are treated as usability requirements.

defining_facts.text: Contextual inquiry is one of many methods for gathering end-user requirements, which in the context of usability requirement gathering are treated as usability requirements.

Contextual inquiry is a method more than 30 years old, whose importance in user-centered design was highlighted in 1988 under the term phenomenological research method, and by the end of the 1990s it had become well developed and popular.
Contextual inquiry is often referred to as a semi-structured interview process that consists of both interviews and observations.

The primary objective of contextual inquiry is to watch and observe users performing tasks in their natural work setting, that is, their work context, in order to gather more insight about user behavior and end-user requirements.
The interview part in contextual inquiry may involve asking users questions during observations to clarify certain behaviors or activities.
A well-planned contextual inquiry process generally takes one to two hours.

Observations and interaction with users in contextual inquiry enable designers to learn about the task domain, work culture, and physical and social constraints at the workplace, which supports design decisions.

Contextual inquiry is important in system development because it studies users, such as managerial staff, in their work setting, reveals their unique behavioral traits, and enables design refinement; without it, designers may create invalid designs and give essential user activities equal importance to unnecessary features, compromising usability.

User activities observed in contextual inquiry must be supported as features in the system design; in the calendar app for managerial staff, the observed activities are setting meeting dates and reminders, so the app must support them to be usable for that user group.
Contextual inquiry is a usability requirement-gathering method that observes targeted or specified groups of users in their natural work setting to understand how they behave and what they do.

Contextual inquiry can be performed in two broad modes: active mode, where the observer is physically present in the environment where the users are doing their tasks, and passive mode, where no observer is present, user activities are recorded or videotaped and later observed by the observer, and issues are clarified through interaction with the users.

In genuine contextual inquiry, the observer must act as an apprentice or learner and treat users as masters or teachers, the master-apprentice model, learning how users behave instead of advising or teaching them how to behave; such advice is prohibited.
The five stages of contextual inquiry are plan, initiate, execute, close, and reflect, in that order, and they provide a systematic way of carrying out the inquiry process.

The plan stage of contextual inquiry involves identifying the goals of observation, gathering knowledge about the task domain, planning arrangements for recording observations, identifying the users and the date, time, and place of the observation, and, as a helpful practice, scripting and rehearsing the procedure.

The initiate stage of contextual inquiry involves obtaining all necessary permissions from relevant authorities before observing employees in their workplace and opening communication with end users to remove anxieties that the observation may lead to something bad for them, so that they behave naturally.
The execute stage of contextual inquiry is the stage in which the actual inquiry takes place, through performing observations and recording data.

The close stage of contextual inquiry ideally involves formally closing by sending thank-you notes or a message of gratitude to the users and possibly the authorities, because such users may be useful for future activities such as usability testing.
The reflect stage of contextual inquiry is the stage in which the observer or experimental team analyzes the data collected during the execute stage and identifies the design goals.

The affinity diagram method is a technique used in the reflect stage of contextual inquiry to arrange the collected data so that patterns can be found more easily, leading to the design specification of the design goals.
The outcome of contextual inquiry, a usability requirement gathering method, can be utilized as design guidelines, design recommendations, or design principles, and also as functional requirements.

Contextual inquiry (CI) in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was conducted after the user groups were identified, on samples from those user groups, to learn their needs and expectations, identify the system features to be supported for each group, and identify specific issues for those groups related to broad design challenges.

The large geographical area and cyber sickness challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was addressed by allowing each user group to access only a subset of the collected data, with each subset identified through contextual inquiry (CI) based on what that group typically does.

Location awareness in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was identified during contextual inquiry (CI) as an issue for users exploring a large space, and a possible resolution was to add a location awareness feature, later to be converted into functional requirements during system design.
Contextual inquiry is one of many methods available for usability requirement gathering.

concepts.name: satra
concepts.definition: Satras are Vaishnavite monasteries on Majuli that are authoritative centers of Vaishnavite faith in Assam and are living workshops of different kinds of visual and performing arts.

defining_facts.text: Satras are Vaishnavite monasteries on Majuli that are authoritative centers of Vaishnavite faith in Assam and are living workshops of different kinds of visual and performing arts.

Tangible heritage of Majuli consists of heritage aspects that someone can touch and feel, such as cultural artifacts like masks and musical instruments and the architectural aspects of Satras and traditional tribal homes.
Satras on Majuli are monasteries of the Vaisnavite faith that contain tangible and intangible cultural aspects, and there are 22 Satras in total.
Auniati Satra is one of the largest, most prominent, and most visited Satras on Majuli, with a campus covering approximately 1200 square meters and at least 25 points of interest.

The Majuli virtual tour contains a large number of geographically spread information points, including satras (Vaishnavite monasteries), villages, tribal villages, towns, and other places of interest, and each information point contains many points of interest, creating two levels of extensive content.

The Majuli multimodal archive consists of regular images, 360-degree images, and videos for the indigenous architectural heritage of satras (Vaishnavite monasteries) and village life, 3D models for landscape and architecture, 2D drone shots for landscape, flora, and fauna, 2D videos for intangible cultural heritage, and textual descriptions.

concepts.name: natural walking speed model
concepts.definition: The natural walking speed model was formed by multiplying computed natural walking behavior by a visual gain factor to let the user perceive natural walking.

defining_facts.text: The natural walking speed model was formed by multiplying computed natural walking behavior by a visual gain factor to let the user perceive natural walking.
The empirical study was carried out to confirm whether the natural walking speed model, described as instantaneous speed, enhances perceived realism compared with a constant average speed.

The empirical study used a virtual art exhibition environment experienced with an Oculus Rift, in which system-controlled navigation moved the user at constant speed or instantaneous natural walking speed through pictures, with a forced 10-second stop at each picture.

Each participant experienced both constant speed and instantaneous speed conditions in a randomized order, with breaks between the conditions, to avoid practice effect and bias in the subsequent data collection.

The study used two 1-to-10 rating scales, with 1 representing worst and 10 representing the best value, to rate level of realism and user preference, and speed with levels constant and instantaneous was the independent variable, with realism and preference as the dependent variables.

Box plots of the realism and preference ratings showed that instantaneous speed produced higher realism ratings and higher user preference than constant speed, and paired sample t-tests with a p-value of 0.05 showed these differences were statistically significant.
The instantaneous natural walking speed model is suitable for a realistic walking experience in controlled virtual reality (VR) tools and is likely to increase presence.

The instantaneous natural walking speed model alone does not address cyber sickness, and the question of how to minimize cyber sickness with only that model cannot be answered, so additional measures are required.
The first stage of the travel-time algorithm is to compute the time to travel between two directly connected nodes using the natural walking-speed model.
In the natural walking-speed model, perceived instantaneous walking speed is the visual gain of 2.1 multiplied by the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act).
In the natural walking-speed model, f is the instantaneous step frequency and h is the height of the user.

After solving the integral with simplifications, rearrangements, and Fourier-series expansion up to n0, the travel-time estimate tau D for a directly connected vertex pair under the natural walking model is D/V naught times (3 - (16/pi^2) * sum_{k=1}^{n0} 1/(2k-1)^2).
V naught is a constant for a given height h, equal to 2.1 h^2 divided by (0.157 * 1.72^2 * 1.8^2), where h is the user's height.

concepts.name: graph
concepts.definition: The algorithm takes the original graph G, with vertex set V and edge set epsilon, as input and produces the optimal time T and the path P of the minimum-time path that covers all vertices in G.

defining_facts.text: The algorithm takes the original graph G, with vertex set V and edge set epsilon, as input and produces the optimal time T and the path P of the minimum-time path that covers all vertices in G.

The algorithm first converts the original graph G into a complete graph G' by keeping every directly connected edge unchanged and, for each pair of vertices that is not directly connected, adding a hypothetical edge whose length is the shortest path between those vertices in G.

After the graph is complete, the algorithm replaces the Euclidean-distance edge weights with the travel time between each pair of vertices, producing a complete time-weighted graph G'' whose edge weights are travel times rather than Euclidean distances.

The complete time-weighted graph G'' can be solved with a standard travelling salesman problem (TSP) solver, without needing a new algorithm, and the solver returns the optimal time tau_opt and the optimal path p_opt for that modified graph.

Because the travelling salesman problem (TSP) solver's optimal path p_opt may contain hypothetical edges that are not in the original graph G, the algorithm post-processes p_opt into p_dash_opt by checking each path edge and replacing each edge whose endpoints were not directly connected in G with the shortest path between those endpoints in G.

The minimum travel time to cover all vertices, as computed by the algorithm that maps the original graph to a travelling salesman problem (TSP) instance, may still exceed the cybersickness time threshold when the terrain or virtual environment is large, so its purpose may be defeated in such cases.

In the minimum-time approach, the virtual world is represented as a graph whose nodes are points of interest, whose directly connected edges are weighted by the Euclidean distance between the corresponding points of interest, and whose graph need not be complete.
The problem of finding the minimum-duration travel that covers all points of interest in the virtual-world graph is mapped to the travelling salesman problem (TSP), a standard classical problem.

The Satra campus is modeled as a graph in which the points of interest (POI) are the nodes, the graph has at least 25 nodes, and the edges connecting pairs of nodes are weighted by the Euclidean distance between the corresponding points of interest.
Converting the Satra site into a graph representation is an iterative process that requires detailed field study and revision of an initial graph.

Once the graph is obtained, a traveling salesman problem (TSP) solver can be used to find a minimum-time path covering all 25 nodes, or a vehicle routing problem with profits (VRPP) solver can be used to find a path within a chosen time threshold that covers the maximum number of most important points of interest while accounting for the maximum wait time at each point of interest.

concepts.name: time threshold
concepts.definition: A time-constrained virtual tour optimization approach seeks an optimal path that covers the maximum number of points of interest (POIs) while completing within the time threshold (TTH).

defining_facts.text: A time-constrained virtual tour optimization approach seeks an optimal path that covers the maximum number of points of interest (POIs) while completing within the time threshold (TTH).

The time threshold (TTH) for cybersickness (CS) is the maximum duration of a virtual reality (VR) tour, meaning the user's movement time, experience time, or VR exposure time should be kept within it, because crossing it may cause cybersickness.

A virtual tour optimized to cover all vertices of a virtual world graph in minimum time may still induce cybersickness (CS) if its traversal time exceeds the threshold above which cybersickness occurs.

There is no easy way to determine the time threshold (TTH); recommended thresholds may depend on content and movement speed, and a threshold can be obtained from an empirical study with a limited number of users or from pre-existing study results.

Vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP) is a generalization of the vehicle routing problem (VRP), an operations research problem, in which not all nodes must be visited and the route maximizes profit within a time constraint, and in this formulation profit is the importance of the nodes.
Existing vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP) solvers can be used to find the optimal path that maximizes total importance of the nodes within the given time threshold.

The optimized path must keep the user's exposure below a time threshold beyond which cybersickness may occur and, within that time, let the user visit as many of the most important points of interest (POIs) as possible.

In a walking-based virtual reality (VR) exploration, the optimal path under a time constraint approach sets an upper time limit, called the time threshold, for the user's exposure to the virtual tour, and within that duration it identifies a path that covers the maximum number of the most important points of interest, where covering includes interacting with or inspecting those points and navigating from one to another.

concepts.name: vehicle routing problem with profit
concepts.definition: Vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP) is a generalization of the vehicle routing problem (VRP), an operations research problem, in which not all nodes must be visited and the route maximizes profit within a time constraint, and in this formulation profit is the importance of the nodes.

defining_facts.text: Vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP) is a generalization of the vehicle routing problem (VRP), an operations research problem, in which not all nodes must be visited and the route maximizes profit within a time constraint, and in this formulation profit is the importance of the nodes.
Existing vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP) solvers can be used to find the optimal path that maximizes total importance of the nodes within the given time threshold.

never_defined.name: virtual world
never_defined.definition: To different people, hearing extended reality (XR), virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), or mixed reality (MR) may lead them to associate one or more of these terms with magical movie scenes such as those in Avatar, interactive video games, 3D or 4D movie-theater documentaries about extinct animals, a user wearing a headset that blocks vision and transports the user to a virtual world, which is the most common perception of VR, games such as Pokémon Go in which the real world is visible on a device screen and virtual objects that do not exist in the real world can also be seen on that screen, or visualizations of internal body structures such as a skeleton or veins.
